name: Big Rip Universe
description: A flat Friedmann universe filled with phantom energy, whose pressure is more negative than minus its energy density. The density grows as space expands, and the scale factor reaches infinity at a finite time, the Big Rip, pulling apart every bound system on the way.
convention: We keep factors of $c$ explicit, and the Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.
history: In 2003 Robert R. Caldwell, Marc Kamionkowski, and Nevin N. Weinberg worked out the end of a universe filled with phantom energy, with $w = p/\rho c^2 = -3/2$: clusters of galaxies erased a billion years before the end, the Milky Way sixty million years before, the solar system unbound three months before, the Earth exploding thirty minutes before, and atoms torn apart $10^{-19}$ seconds before [caldwell2003]. Phantom energy grows denser as the universe expands, since its pressure $p$ is more negative than minus its energy density $\rho c^2$ [caldwell2003]. The expansion speeds up with it, and the scale factor reaches infinity a finite time from now, about 22 billion years for $w = -3/2$ and a Hubble rate of $70$ km/s/Mpc today [caldwell2003]. They named that moment the Big Rip, and wrote that the slogan of "cosmic futurologists", Robert Frost's "Some say the world will end in fire, Some say in ice", would have to change, "for a new fate may await our world" [caldwell2003, nojiri2005].¶The phantom itself is four years older, the work of Caldwell alone at Dartmouth College in August 1999 [caldwell2002]. Most observations of the day allowed every equation of state right down to $w = -1$, the cosmological constant, and Caldwell asked "what lies on the other side of this boundary" [caldwell2002]. He called the new component a phantom, "something which is apparent to the sight or other senses but has no corporeal existence" [caldwell2002]. His toy model is a scalar field with the sign of its kinetic term switched, so that the field runs up its potential toward larger energy [caldwell2002]. Its scale factor already diverges at a finite time: for $w = -3$, in a universe ruled by matter until a time $t_m$, at $t = 3t_m/2$ [caldwell2002].¶That December the same ending turned up on a list of possible futures drawn up by Alexei A. Starobinsky, at the Landau Institute in Moscow: "hitting a space-time singularity during an expansion phase" [starobinsky2000]. For a constant $w < -1$ he worked out how long the universe has left, and with the bound $w > -1.5$ from the supernovae he found more than 22 billion years [starobinsky2000]. The name Big Smash came from Brett McInnes, at the National University of Singapore, in 2002: "Instead of suffering a 'crunch', the universe is 'smashed'" [mcinnes2002]. He also built phantom universes that escape it, with a $w$ that changes in time, which settle into de Sitter space at late times [mcinnes2002].¶Why would a phantom tear apart a solar system that a cosmological constant leaves alone? In general relativity the pull of gravity comes from the density plus three times the pressure, and a planet on an orbit of radius $R$ about a star of mass $M$ comes loose roughly when $-(4\pi/3)(\rho + 3p)R^3 \simeq M$, in units with $G = c = 1$ [caldwell2003]. For $w \geq -1$ the left side only shrinks as the universe expands, so whatever is bound today stays bound [caldwell2003]. For a phantom it grows without limit, and every bound system comes apart a time $P\sqrt{2|1 + 3w|}/(6\pi|1 + w|)$ before the end, with $P$ the period of its orbit, whatever the Hubble rate and the amount of matter [caldwell2003]. The horizon closes in at the same time, and two points farther apart than $3c\,\delta t\,(1 + w)/(1 + 3w)$ a time $\delta t$ before the end can no longer signal each other [caldwell2003].¶In a survey of the futures of universes with dark energy in 2005, Takeshi Chiba, Ryuichi Takahashi, and Naoshi Sugiyama drew the conformal diagram [chiba2005]. With phantom energy alone it is the lower half of Minkowski space's diagram, as de Sitter space's is, with the Big Rip along its top edge at future spacelike infinity [chiba2005]. Every observer has an event horizon, and with the rip at $t = 0$ its proper radius $3(1 + w)(-ct)/(1 + 3w)$ shrinks to nothing there [chiba2005]. In the four types of ending sorted out the same year by Shin'ichi Nojiri, Sergei D. Odintsov, and Shinji Tsujikawa, the Big Rip is type I, where the scale factor, the density, and the pressure all diverge [nojiri2005].¶Type II is the sudden singularity of John D. Barrow, at Cambridge, from 2004 [nojiri2005, barrow2004]. There the scale factor, the expansion rate, and the density all stay finite, and only the pressure and the acceleration diverge, even with $\rho > 0$ and $\rho + 3p/c^2 > 0$ [barrow2004]. When Leonardo Fernández-Jambrina and Ruth Lazkoz followed geodesics into it, the geodesics ran on through, and the tidal forces were "not strong enough to produce a Big Rip" [fernandezjambrina2004]. The spacetime carries on beyond a sudden singularity, and a body that crosses it is not necessarily torn apart [fernandezjambrina2004]. At a Big Rip the scale factor and all of its derivatives blow up, and structure is destroyed [fernandezjambrina2004].

related.text: Friedmann's universe with its scale factor left free and its space allowed to curve. Its flat case filled with phantom energy alone is this universe [chiba2005].

The limit $w \to -1$, with the expansion rate at $a = 1$ held fixed: the Big Rip moves off to infinite time, and the scale factor becomes de Sitter's exponential. Both conformal diagrams are the lower half of Minkowski space's [chiba2005].
A wormhole held open by a scalar field whose kinetic term has the opposite of the usual sign, the kind of field Robert Caldwell used for his phantom energy [ellis1973, caldwell2002].

A black hole whose singularity opens into a bounce. Kirill Bronnikov and Rahul Kumar Walia found it a source in a phantom scalar field with a potential and a magnetic field, and the phantom field is the kind behind phantom energy [bronnikov2022, caldwell2002].

coordinates.name: Comoving Cartesian

parameters.description: Equation of state of the phantom energy, $w = p/\rho c^2 < -1$, with $\rho$ its mass density and $p$ its pressure
Time left before the Big Rip at the moment $a = 1$, $t_0 = 2/(3|1 + w|H_0)$ with $H_0$ the Hubble rate at that moment
Scale factor, equal to $1$ at $t = -t_0$ and growing without bound as $t \to 0$; the Hubble rate is $H = 2/(3(1 + w)t)$

coordinates.convention: We use comoving coordinates $(t, x, y, z)$, with $t$ the proper time of a comoving observer, negative before the Big Rip at $t = 0$, and $x$, $y$, and $z$ lengths, the proper distances at $t = -t_0$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

coordinates.convention: We use comoving coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$, with $t$ the proper time of a comoving observer, negative before the Big Rip at $t = 0$, and $r$ a length, the proper radius at $t = -t_0$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

coordinates.name: Conformal

parameters.description: Equation of state of the phantom energy, $w = p/\rho c^2 < -1$, with $\rho$ its mass density and $p$ its pressure
A length, $\eta_0 = 3(1 + w)ct_0/(1 + 3w)$, the conformal time left before the Big Rip at the moment $a = 1$
Scale factor, equal to $1$ at $\eta = -\eta_0$ and growing without bound as $\eta \to 0$

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(\eta, r, \theta, \phi)$, with $\eta$ the conformal time, a length with $d\eta = c\,dt/a$ that is negative before the Big Rip at $\eta = 0$, and $r$ the comoving radius, a length. We take components in the chart $x^0 = \eta$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter.
